I have attempted in the past to build addons written in NativeScript C++, but the process is cumbersome and concerns me at scale.

results.title: Add PR-style review comments in Git Diff UI that feed into the active agent thread
results.body_snippet:
### Discussed in https://github.com/zed-industries/zed/discussions/54663

<div type='discussions-op-text'>

<sup>Originally posted by **GoodnessDev** April 23, 2026</sup>
# What are you proposing?

I am proposing PR-style review comments directly in Zed's Git Diff UI, where human comments on a file, hunk, or line get fed into the currently active agent thread as structured feedback.

This is not the same as "attach the current diff to the thread" or "ask AI to review the diff".
The key workflow is the other direction:

1. I review the local diff in Zed's Git UI.
2. I leave one or more targeted comments, like I would on a GitHub PR.
3. Those comments are sent into the active agent session/thread.
4. The agent can respond to the comments and make follow-up edits.

Example:
- I open a Git diff in Zed.
- On a hunk, I leave a comment: `This rename breaks the public API. Keep the old name and add an overload instead.`
- That comment becomes a new message or structured feedback event in the active agent thread, with the relevant file/hunk context attached.
- The agent then addresses that exact review feedback.

The VSCode extension automatically includes every file I open or switch to as conversation context for Claude. results.body_snippet:
# Summary

Hello! I'm on the evals team at Poolside AI and we've been heavily using SWE-Bench Pro internally for benchmarking our model development, lately we have been deeply reviewing model performance on the benchmark. While reviewing recent model runs on SWE-Bench Pro, I found a reward hacking exploit in the SWE-Bench Pro Open Source dataset via future git history mining. 

This exploit is very similar in shape to the problem reported in SWE-Bench Verified last year: https://github.com/SWE-bench/SWE-bench/issues/465. 

Specifically, the public OSS Docker images on DockerHub (and any subsequent builds from the Dockerfiles in the SWE-Bench Pro repo):
1. Do not sufficiently remove future commit history on the main branch which can leak the solution
2. Feature branches, such as `origin/dev`, contain future commits and are discoverable by agents with sufficient exploration. 
   - Looks like this concern was raised in #7 but not clearly proven to be exploited (example below)
3. Git tags are also available that leak the same content (although I didn't see this come up in review, I was able to manually confirm it in images)

This means all a model really needs to do is `git show <fix>`

results.title: Improving the developer experience with regard to default string globalization
results.body_snippet:
## Improving the developer experience with regard to default string globalization

> Note: This is a companion document to https://github.com/dotnet/docs/issues/21249, which discusses the behaviors as they currently exist. It's assumed the reader is generally familiar with that document.

### Summary

Since .NET 5 standardized on using ICU instead of NLS for globalization across all supported platforms (see [breaking change notice](https://docs.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/compatibility/globalization#globalization-apis-use-icu-libraries-on-windows)), we've received a few reports of `string` and globalization APIs not behaving as expected.

These reports generally fall into one of two buckets:

1. The developer wasn't intending to make their code globalization-aware, and the switch to ICU exposed an unintentional dependency in the developer's code which led to an unwanted behavioral change. See: https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/43736, https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/42234, https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/40922, https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/40258, https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/36177, https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/3399

results.title: [FEATURE] Desktop app: setting to auto-expand Edit/Write diffs by default
results.body_snippet:
### Feature Request

In the Claude Code desktop app, Edit/Write tool calls render with the diff collapsed by default. Reviewing a conversation that contains multiple edits requires clicking each diff card individually to see what changed.

Add a setting (e.g. `desktop.diffs.expandedByDefault: true` in `~/.claude/settings.json`, or a toggle in the desktop app preferences UI) that renders every Edit/Write diff in the expanded state from the start.

### Use Case

When reviewing a session — either live as Claude works, or scrolling back through a completed conversation — I want to see what was changed without clicking. The collapsed-by-default behavior optimizes for vertical density at the cost of every-diff being a manual interaction. For users who care more about reviewing changes than skimming a long transcript, the inverse default is more useful.

This is especially noticeable in sessions with many small edits (refactors, fixups, codegen passes) where the cost of expanding each one adds up quickly.

### Suggested Behavior

- A user preference (settings.json key and/or preferences UI toggle) that defaults all Edit/Write diff cards to expanded state on render.
- Should apply to both

results.title: Feature request: Git blame / line annotation in the editor
results.body_snippet:
## Summary

It would be great to have **git blame** support directly in Orca's built-in file editor — showing, for each line, the author, commit hash, and date of the last change.

## Motivation

When reviewing AI-generated code or navigating an existing codebase, it's often useful to know:
- Who last touched a given line (or which agent/commit introduced it)
- When the change was made
- Which commit it belongs to (with the ability to jump to that commit)

Today, the only workaround is to run `git blame <file>` manually in the integrated terminal, which breaks the flow of reviewing diffs or editing code inside Orca.

## Proposed behaviour

- **Inline gutter annotations**: show a compact blame tooltip or inline text (author + date + short commit hash) next to each line, similar to GitLens in VS Code or the "Annotate" view in JetBrains IDEs.
- **On-demand**: triggered by a keyboard shortcut or right-click context menu (e.g. "Show git blame"), so it doesn't clutter the editor by default.
- **Click to inspect**: clicking an annotation would open the full commit details (message, diff, author).

## Additional context

This would complement the existing **Annotate AI Diff** feature nicel
